label: Reconstructed 1904 coachman's standing livery (double-breasted livery coat to the knee with two rows of white-metal buttons, white stock, white gloves, white breeches, black top boots, silk top hat) on the shared portable male rig
basis: Original livery-coat shells offset from the cleared adult body's own surface, its skirt lofted round its sections, buttons laid on the coat, a stock lofted round the neck, gloves offset from the hands, breeches from the legs, boot shafts lofted round the calves, a top hat seated round the skull and closed shoes round the feet, cut after the coachman's livery the reference pictures show (T-3483). Seams, ease, lengths and colours are reconstructed. Complete source anatomy remains unchanged beneath clothing.
source_scope: The 'Coachman' plate of Mrs. Seely's Cook Book (New York, 1902) shows a private coachman standing full length in his livery: a double-breasted coat buttoned to the throat and falling to the knee, two rows of six bright buttons, a white stock, white gloves, white breeches showing above black top boots, a silk hat; its mourning plate the same coat on an older man. The Griffith (1905) and Rau (1902) stereographs show coachmen of the decade in double-breasted coats with bright buttons, stand collars, white stocks and silk hats; Penfield's drawing shows a brougham coachman's livery in colour (a light coat, light breeches and top boots), so livery was coloured, not only black. None is of Chicago or of Nelson; all the photographs are monochrome; no pixels or traced shapes enter the asset.

proof_variants.body_basis: CC0 adult-male graphical body and the older light-skinned generic skin of the 1904 gentleman are reconstructed authoring choices. Charles Nelson is an inferred person (the 1900 census enumerates him as the Glessners' coachman in the rear building); no picture of him is known, and no complexion, height, face or outfit of his is asserted.

coachman_components.evidence_choice: The brief asked for a coachman standing at his own stable in a livery distinct from Hans Johnson's box coat and cape. The Seely plate is the one picture read of a private coachman standing in livery in these years, and every piece is taken from it: the double-breasted coat to the knee, two rows of buttons, stock, white gloves, breeches, top boots and silk hat. No cape and no box coat (those are for the box); bottle green and white metal instead of Hans's dark blue and brass.

provenance.source_scope: The Seely coachman (1902) wears a double-breasted coat buttoned to the throat with a low collar, falling straight to the knee; the Griffith coachmen (1905) wear double-breasted coats with stand collars. That Nelson wore such a coat is not recorded; its dark bottle green is reconstructed (the photographs are monochrome; Penfield's coloured livery shows that a household's livery had its own colour), chosen to differ from Hans Johnson's dark blue.

Two rows of six bright buttons from the chest to the waist, the rows a little wider apart at the top, as the Seely plate shows; the Griffith coachmen's buttons read bright too. White metal (not brass) is reconstructed.
A white stock standing above the coat's collar, as on the Seely and Rau coachmen; its height and linen are reconstructed.
White gloves, as the Seely coachman and the Griffith coachmen wear; cotton is reconstructed.
White breeches showing a hand's breadth between the coat's hem and the boot tops (Seely; Penfield draws light breeches); their fullness over the thigh is reconstructed.
Plain black boots to just below the knee (Seely; Penfield's top boots); their stiffness and fit are reconstructed.
A tall silk hat with a narrow curled brim, as every coachman of the set wears; its exact crown and brim are reconstructed.
